The main historical sequence

The early-medieval period is easier to understand when political change, agrarian expansion and external contacts are placed in one chronological sequence. The following dates identify major developments rather than every event in the period.

738–739Resistance to an Arab advance near NavsariAvanijanashraya Pulakeshin

Essential ruler-place pairs

The most useful associations can be grouped by region. Distinguishing the type of association is important: some places were capitals, some were cultural centres and others were battle sites.

Connecting political, economic and cultural history

The developments covered in this lesson were interrelated. Regional rulers needed resources to maintain courts, armies and officials. Agricultural expansion and irrigation increased the potential revenue available to states and institutions.

Land grants transferred specified rights and helped support religious institutions, local elites and sometimes military supporters. Temples could become centres of employment and settlement. Powerful subordinate chiefs could develop their own ruling houses, adding to the number of competing regional states.

At the same time, maritime trade connected the subcontinent with Arabia and other regions. Military expansion from the north-west brought a different form of interaction. Arab authority in Sindh, Ghaznavid campaigns and Ghurid conquests each had distinct territorial consequences.

Five distinctions that prevent common errors

  • Samanta versus independent ruler: A samanta acknowledged an overlord; independence involved asserting separate sovereign authority.
  • Land grant versus ownership of all rights: A grant transferred the rights specified in its terms; it did not always replace cultivators or transfer every possible right.
  • Rajput polity versus single Rajput empire: Different clans and dynasties ruled separate territories and could be political rivals.
  • Tripartite struggle versus Tarain: The former involved Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas competing for Kanauj; the latter involved Prithviraja III and Muhammad Ghori.
  • Ghaznavid versus Ghurid: Mahmud of Ghazni is particularly associated with repeated raids and the Somnath campaign; Muhammad Ghori is associated with Tarain, Chandawar and the conquests preceding the Delhi Sultanate.

Prelims focus

  • Kanauj was the focus of the tripartite struggle involving the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas.
  • Brahmadeya, devadana and shalabhoga identify different purposes or beneficiaries of land grants.
  • Chahamanas are associated with Ajmer; Paramaras with Dhar; Chandelas with Khajuraho.
  • Somnath, 1025–1026: Mahmud of Ghazni. Gujarat, 1178: defeat of Muhammad Ghori.
  • Tarain, 1191: Prithviraja III won. Tarain, 1192: Muhammad Ghori won.
  • Trap: The Ghurid victory in 1192 and the beginning of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 were related but separate events.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 11, 'New Empires and Kingdoms', printed pp. 116–120; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, chs. 1–2, 'Tracing Changes Through a Thousand Years' and 'New Kings and Kingdoms', printed pp. 6–27; GCERT, Social Science, Class 7, ch. 1, 'Rajput Age: New Ruler and States'; GCERT, History, Class 11, ch. 13, 'Rajput States of India', printed pp. 101–103; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, ch. 6, 'Temple Architecture and Sculpture', printed pp. 73–76 and 85–86; IGNOU, BHIM-162, Unit 4, 'Islamic Invasions and Bharatiya States (8th–12th Century CE)' (online, consulted 19 November 2026); UNESCO, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, Volume IV, K. A. Nizami, 'The Ghurids', printed pp. 187–189 (online, consulted 19 November 2026).]
